extracted.intended_audience: painters, art students, and critics studying depiction of water (landscape & marine painters)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for observing and painting the appearance of water (ponds, rivers, seas) in landscape and marine painting, emphasizing optical laws, on‑the‑spot observation, and when (if ever) artistic 'licenses' are permissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithful depiction of reflections
rubrics_metrics.description: 'It is not often, I believe, that an artist draws the reflections in water as he sees them; over large spaces, and in weather that is not very calm, it is nearly impossible to do so; when it is possible, sometimes in haste, and sometimes in idleness, and sometimes under the idea of improving nature, they are slurred or misrepresented.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not 'improve' or lazily indicate water at home; avoid slurring or misrepresenting reflections. Anti‑patterns: finishing water from memory with cold leaden grays, violent blues/greens, horizontal lines, or decorative bright touches that give something 'like' water but betray ignorance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict submerged landscape as fully as the landscape above
rubrics_metrics.description: 'There is hardly a roadside pond or pool which has not as much landscape in it as above it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw everything you see in the water—trees, shaking leaves, hazy passages of sunlight, bottom details (stones, blades of grass), clouds 'far down in the middle'—often more delicately than the actual objects above. The great painter sees and follows what lies beneath the surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study common/dirty ponds thoroughly on the spot
rubrics_metrics.description: 'If painters would only go out to the nearest common and take the nearest dirty pond ... and draw that thoroughly ... they would come home with such a notion of water-painting ...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On‑the‑spot, determined study of even ugly/ polluted water teaches complex effects that studio finish cannot substitute. Portfolios of immediate water studies are more valuable than analytic optical knowledge alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid beautifying polluted water with coarse colors
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Instead of giving that refined, complex, delicate, but saddened and gloomy reflection in the polluted water, they clear it up with coarse flashes of yellow, and green, and blue, and spoil their own eyes, and hurt ours.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting foul or polluted water, seek refined, complex, and subdued reflections rather than bright, coarse color patches. Respect the water's real 'sad' tonal quality; do not substitute prettiness for truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angle dependence: reflective power vs transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: First rule: '...a surface whose reflective power is dependent on the angle at which the rays to be reflected fall. The smaller this angle, the greater are the number of rays reflected...the visible transparency and reflective power of water are in inverse ratio.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that looking along water increases reflection (images of objects above), while looking down increases transmission (showing bottom/objects in the water). Shallow water shows bottom near the spectator and loses it with distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local color modifies dark reflections but not bright ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Second rule: 'The brighter the objects reflected, the larger the angle at which reflection is visible...only light objects are reflected, and the darker ones are seen only in proportion to the number of rays ... so that a dark object comparatively loses its power to affect the surface of water.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect dark objects to be partially lost and to mix with the water's own hue; bright objects are reflected more purely. Use this to create subtle color variety—dark reflections often show the water's local color (example: black hulls reflected as pale sea green in Venice diary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear water 'takes no shadow' — apparent shadows are often reflections
rubrics_metrics.description: Third rule: 'Clear water takes no shadow, and that for two reasons...a perfectly transparent body as air takes no shadow; hence water ... takes no shadow.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not render shadows on water as simply darker patches like on land. Apparent shadows often arise from increased reflectiveness in shade, or from reflection of dark sky/objects. Painting 'shadows' requires considering reflection, local color, and transmitted light rather than simple darkening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shadows affect dark and bright reflections differently (and apparent vs real shadows)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Hence when a shadow is thrown across a space of water of strong local color ... it has no power of increasing the reflectiveness of the water in the bright spaces, still less of diminishing it; hence, on all the dark reflections it is seen more or less distinctly, on all the light ones it vanishes altogether.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a shadow crosses mixed reflections, model its effect relative to underlying reflection: it will manifest over dark reflections, disappear over bright ones. Also, particulate/foul water can take 'real' shadow; rippled surfaces produce spotty sun images whose withdrawal creates apparent shadows. Account for these causes when painting shaded areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ripples: nearer side reflects sky, farther side reflects shore; distant rippled surface reads as sky-only
rubrics_metrics.description: Fourth rule: 'If water be rippled, the side of every ripple next to us reflects a piece of the sky, and the side of every ripple farthest from us reflects a piece of the opposite shore...the whole rippled surface will then be reflective of the sky only.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect ripples to interrupt long-distance reflections of shores by inserting bands of sky color; in practice, distant rippled areas often appear as bright lines or breaks in otherwise shore-reflecting surfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion elongates reflections into vertical lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Fifth rule: 'Therefore all motion in water elongates reflections, and throws them into confused vertical lines...especially of lights, as of the sun, moon, or lamps by a river shore, whose reflections are hardly ever seen as circles or points, ... but as long streams of tremulous light.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict moving-water reflections as vertically elongated, tremulous streams rather than point images. Expect elongation to be very pronounced for bright objects (sun, lights, white sails); spectators may mistrust accurate elongation, but it is true to observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rippled water preserves perpendicular lines but confuses sloping/horizontal ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Sixth rule: 'Rippled water ... will reflect a perpendicular line clearly ... But if the line slope, its reflection will be excessively confused and disjointed; and if horizontal, nearly invisible.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When painting objects with strong horizontal markings (e.g., ship stripes), recognize they may disappear on rippled water; perpendicular elements (masts, towers) will read more clearly in reflections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of visible reflection depends on observer height (shortening of reflections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seventh rule: 'Every reflection is the image in reverse of just so much of the objects beside the water, as we could see if we were placed as much under the level of the water as we are actually above it...Hence the reflection of all objects that have any slope back from the water is shortened, and at last disappears as we rise above it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose reflections with viewpoint in mind: from high vantage points lakes reflect sky but not shores; reflections of shore objects shorten or vanish as spectator height increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deflection of images on sloping/agitated water; practical remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Eighth rule: 'On rippled water a slight deflection sometimes takes place, and the image of a vertical tower will slope a little away from the wind...On the sloping sides of large waves the deflection is in proportion to the slope.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To paint reflections on sloping wave faces, determine the slope then 'turn the paper until it becomes horizontal, and then paint the reflections ... as on level water'—a practical tip to correct apparent deflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watchfulness and on‑the‑spot sketches matter more than analytic knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Constant and eager watchfulness, and portfolios filled with actual statements of water-effect, drawn on the spot and on the instant, are worth more to the painter than the most extended optical knowledge.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate observational habit: frequent quick studies from life capture transient, inexplicable effects that formal rules cannot fully predict. Use science to inform but not replace direct seeing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic 'licenses' may be permissible but depend on spirit and authority
rubrics_metrics.description: 'An artist may know all these laws, and comply with them, and yet paint water execrably; and he may be ignorant of every one of them ... and yet paint water gloriously.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licenses (optical departures) are judged by intent and artistic power—when taken from strength they may be admirable; when from fear or incompetence they are condemnable. Distinguish courageous, meaningful departures (Tintoret's shadow-of-light example) from cowardly evasions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid monotonous, formulaic ripple symbols (Canaletto critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'He almost always covers the whole space of it with one monotonous ripple ... a coat of well‑chosen ... sea‑green, covered with ... white concave touches ...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on formulaic, repetitive white touches to indicate water; such mechanical devices can mask ignorance and produce false spatial/reflective effects (e.g., Canaletto's increasing distant object reflections contrary to optical rules). Vary treatment according to optical principles, distance, and motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not render water as a flat plate of metal or bad mirror
rubrics_metrics.description: (Paul Potter critique) '...there is something wrong with the water, that it looks odd, and hard, and like ice or lead; ... the reason is ... it reflects none of the cows.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making water appear like a mirror‑plate; ensure water integrates with the scene—if cows are above and should be reflected, their absence makes the surface feel false. Keep liquidity and transmissive properties intact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not sacrifice liquidity for a manufactured sense of distance (Vandevelde critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Vandevelde evidently desired to give an impression of great extent of surface ... he is not on that account to be excused for painting his surface with gray horizontal lines ... for no destruction of distance in the ocean is so serious a loss as that of its liquidity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid horizontal gray banding or other devices that make the sea feel walkable or like a flat plane. Preserve the sea's liquidity even if that complicates conveying distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paint sea highlights, foam, and cast shadows correctly in rough water
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Every large wave ... is ... covered by innumerable smaller waves, each of which ... reflects the sunbeams; hence result a glitter, polish, and vigorous light over the whole flank of the wave ... every string and wreath of foam above or within the wave takes real shadow.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In rough seas paint masses of glittering highlights on the wave flanks, and treat foam as taking real shadow (unlike smooth surface). Model the withdrawal of high lights within apparent cast shadows to show form without misrepresenting optical cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: When painting 'shadows' on water consider all affecting circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Whenever we have to paint such shadows, it is not only the hue of the water itself that we have to consider, but all the circumstances by which in the position attributed to them such shaded spaces could be affected.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for local color, transmitted light, increased reflectiveness in shade, particulate matter, rippling, and relative positions of sky/objects when rendering shaded areas on water—do not rely on a single tonal rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errors reveal an underlying spirit of mind—avoid cowardly, blunt feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: 'It is not the mistake or the license itself ... it is the spirit and habit of mind in which the license is taken, the cowardice or bluntness of feeling, which infects every part alike, and deprives the whole picture of vitality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate water painting not only by technical correctness but by the painter's intentions and conviction: technically forgivable departures are excused when the painter's spirit, invention, and courage enliven the work; mechanical evasions reflect poor artistic temperament.
